newsitem.title: JORDAN: Prosecutors say Jordanian planned to kill Israelis.
newsitem.headline: Prosecutors say Jordanian planned to kill Israelis.

text.p: Prosecutors urged a military court on Saturday to sentence "in accordance with the law" a Jordanian soldier charged with premeditated murder of seven Israeli schoolgirls.
Muhannad Hejazi said army private Ahmed Daqamsa, who shot the girls at a border post in March, had planned to attack Israelis for years and carefully prepared for the shooting.

In a tough summary of the prosecution case, Hejazi lashed out at Daqamsa's supporters and disputed his defence that he was a pious man suffering from a mental illness, who shot the girls in a blind fury because they teased him while he was at prayer.
"He murdered unarmed children, who committed no crime except that their fate led them at that moment to be in front of this coward," Hejazi said.
He did not say how Daqamsa should be punished but the charge of premeditated murder carries a possible death sentence.
Daqamsa, looking composed behind the black bars of his cage in the dock, shook his head occasionally but only once briefly interrupted Hejazi's one and a half hour summary.
Hejazi said Daqamsa asked for a rifle and extra ammunition on the day of the shooting, at the border territory of Baqoura which Jordan leased to Israel under their 1994 peace treaty.
He said Daqamsa hinted at his plans to one of his army comrades on the morning of the killing and smiled at another as he loaded his rifle just seconds before opening fire.

"One of the hardest matters and heaviest burdens on us...is that in this case (the defendant) is one of the Arab army, the army of honour," Hejazi said, echoing King Hussein's expression of shame at the shooting.

Jordan's monarch, who has championed his country's peace with Israel after a 46-year state of belligerence, said that Daqamsa should have been shot dead on the spot when he opened fire on the Israelis.
But opponents of the peace treaty have rallied to defend Daqamsa, saying his actions were the result of provocation and deep patriotic instincts fuelled by the long years of conflict with Israel.
"What strange irony in attaching the label of heroism to a deviant pervert who is outside the value system of society," Hejazi said.
He said Daqamsa's supporters had "fraudulently taken it upon themselves to act as guardians of this society... and practised terrorism by misleading public opinion" about Daqamsa.
"They justify the crime with reasons which are flimsier than a spider's web," he said.

Hejazi said psychologists called by the defence had misled the court and contradicted themselves. He quoted at length from medical journals to dispute defence claims that Daqamsa was mentally ill and not responsible for his actions.
"An anti-social personality disorder... is not a mental illness," he said. "Someone with this personality realises wrong and right and the consequences of his actions."
Daqamsa's defence team will sum up their case to the five-man panel of military judges next Saturday.
